claims.text: The relatively low hardness and strength of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi despite good ductility are governed by its degree of short-range atomic order.
A lower level of short-range order provides low barriers to dislocation motion.
Low barriers to dislocation motion enhance plasticity and machinability.
A lower level of short-range order provides insufficient dislocation pinning, resulting in low hardness and strength.
As-cast or standard-annealed equimolar CoCrFeNiTi is a single solid solution with low or minimal short-range order.
An intermediate-temperature thermal treatment can enhance local short-range ordering without inducing a phase change.
The alloy can remain a single-phase solid solution throughout testing from 25 °C to 600 °C under quasi-static loading.
Short-range order in CoCrFeNiTi is reflected by local elemental clustering or subtle ordering, especially involving Ti.
The degree of short-range order can be quantified using high-resolution diffraction or atom-probe tomography.
Enhanced short-range order increases local lattice distortions.
The local lattice distortions associated with enhanced short-range order act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
Greater obstruction of dislocation motion increases hardness and compressive strength.
Enhanced short-range order may limit ductility.
A treatment that measurably enhances short-range order will increase hardness and yield strength relative to the untreated alloy.
A treatment that enhances short-range order may reduce ductility relative to the untreated alloy.
Untreated equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has inherent low short-range order, moderate hardness and strength, and high plasticity and machinability.
The proposed mechanism applies only to equimolar or nearly equimolar, single-phase CoCrFeNiTi tested from 25 °C to 600 °C under quasi-static loading.
Precise identification and quantification of short-range order present experimental challenges.

contradictions.description: Reduced ductility is presented only as a possible outcome, but the falsification rule treats failure to observe the expected ductility reduction as sufficient to falsify the hypothesis.
